Hers
HURZ
pronoun (possessive of she)
Anglo-Saxon hire, possessive form of heo, she — belonging to her.

Biblical Definition

If the firstborn son be hers that was hated. Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field. As though they were not hers.

Hers marks legal or maternal claim in each of its uses, and every instance concerns a woman whose rightful claim is at risk of being overridden. Moses' law in Deuteronomy protects the unloved wife's firstborn son, hers that was hated, from being disinherited in favor of a favored wife's son — birthright determined by birth order, not by the father's preference. The Shunammite woman's restored property — all that was hers — comes only after Gehazi's intervention forces the king's hand, Elisha's earlier kindness to her finally paying out in full during famine and exile. Job's most severe image inverts the pattern entirely: the ostrich, hardened against her young ones, treats them as though they were not hers, a mother's natural claim on her offspring deliberately, almost cruelly, suspended by the Creator's own design.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from HER: possessive pronoun; belonging to her; used absolutely without a following noun.

expand to see more

HER, pron. The objective and possessive case of She.

HERS, pron. The absolute possessive of She; used without a following noun, as, the field is hers.

Distinguished from her (adjective) in that hers stands alone, the possessed thing understood.

Applied in Scripture to inheritance rights (Deuteronomy), restored property (2 Kings), and a mother's claim on her young (Job).

In each instance the word marks a claim of ownership or right that is contested or at risk.

Key Scripture

Deu 21:15 — "If a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated, and they have born him children, both the beloved and the hated; and if the firstborn son be hers that was hated:"

2Ki 8:6 — "And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed unto her a certain officer, saying, Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now."

Job 39:16 — "She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers: her labour is in vain without fear;"

Modern Corruption

Modern inheritance disputes are often settled by sentiment or preference alone; Deuteronomy 21:15-17 stands against exactly this, protecting an unloved wife's firstborn son by objective law regardless of the father's personal feeling.

expand to see more

A culture that prizes personal preference above all else struggles with a law that overrides a father's evident favoritism by fixed birthright rule. Deuteronomy 21 will not let a husband's love for one wife disinherit the legitimate firstborn of another, whatever his private feelings.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical justice often overrides sentiment with fixed, objective rule precisely to protect the vulnerable from a stronger party's shifting preference.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Job 39:16's as though they were not hers renders lo lah (Heb.), not hers, part of God's extended speech from the whirlwind naming the ostrich's strange, divinely-appointed lack of wisdom toward her own young.

expand to see more

Hers in Deuteronomy protects an unloved wife's firstborn by fixed law, not paternal sentiment.

Hers in 2 Kings is restored property, the fruit of Elisha's earlier kindness finally repaid.

Hers in Job describes a mother's claim deliberately suspended in the ostrich by God's own design.

The Job passage belongs to the LORD's extended speech from the whirlwind on creation's strange wisdom.

In each case hers names a claim of right that is contested, protected, or withheld by design.

Usage

"The firstborn son be hers that was hated — protected inheritance rights under Mosaic law."

"Restore all that was hers — the Shunammite woman's property returned after famine."

"As though they were not hers — the ostrich's strange, God-appointed lack of maternal instinct."
